lead: A GNSS receiver computes position from ranges to satellites. The ranges are not perfect; each carries a small error. The spread of satellites across the sky decides how much those range errors grow into position errors. Satellites bunched in one part of the sky give a weak fix. Satellites spread widely give a strong fix. Surveyors measure this spread with DOP, the dilution of precision, and plan observation windows with it. The same numbers help compare a GNSS fix with a total station fix on a project.
prereq: You need: GPS and GNSS: principles and positioning methods for how ranges give position, and weights and adjustment of observations for covariance and error propagation.

blocks.text: Each satellite has an elevation angle above the horizon and an azimuth angle clockwise from north. A skyplot draws azimuth around a circle and elevation as distance from the centre: centre is zenith, outer edge is horizon. Good geometry means satellites are spread in azimuth and include both high and low elevations. A satellite directly overhead adds little horizontal strength; two satellites close together add almost the same information. Range distance itself does not improve geometry.

Let u<sub>i</sub> = (u<sub>x</sub>, u<sub>y</sub>, u<sub>z</sub>) be the unit vector from receiver to satellite i. For four unknowns, x, y, z and receiver clock, the design matrix H has one row per satellite, [-u<sub>x</sub>, -u<sub>y</sub>, -u<sub>z</sub>, 1]. The covariance of the position solution is σ<sub>r</sub>² (HᵀH)⁻¹, where σ<sub>r</sub> is the 1-sigma range error in metres. DOP factors are square roots of diagonal terms of Q = (HᵀH)⁻¹.

blocks.where: σ_position is the 1-sigma position error in metres; DOP is the chosen dilution factor; σ_range is the 1-sigma range error in metres.

items: GDOP = √trace(Q), using x, y, z and clock.
PDOP uses x, y, z. HDOP uses x, y. VDOP uses z. TDOP uses clock.
If satellites lie in one direction, HᵀH is nearly singular and DOP becomes very large.
DOP depends on angular spread, not signal strength.

blocks.text: Precision is repeatability; accuracy is closeness to true coordinates. DOP predicts precision from geometry only. A bias such as an ionospheric delay shifts every fix and is not reduced by good DOP. Report both.

items: RMS: for n horizontal errors e<sub>i</sub>, RMS = √(Σe<sub>i</sub>²/n). It includes bias if present.
CEP is the radius of a circle containing 50% of horizontal fixes. CEP is not 95%.
2DRMS = 2 × DRMS; it contains about 95 % to 98 % of horizontal fixes depending on the shape of the error ellipse (about 98 % when the errors are circular), so it is quoted as a 95 % measure.
Vertical error uses VDOP × σ_range; it is often larger than horizontal error in GPS.

blocks.text: A confidence level states the probability contained. A 95% horizontal radius is about 2DRMS. A 95% vertical interval uses 1.96 σ<sub>v</sub>, where σ<sub>v</sub> is the vertical 1-sigma error. For survey control, compare measured check points, not only DOP.

sections.h3: Error sources, mask angle and planning

blocks.text: Range errors enter every satellite. Some cancel in the position solution; some do not.

items: Ionosphere: free-electron delay, frequency dependent; dual-frequency helps.
Troposphere: dry and wet delay; models reduce it.
Multipath: reflected signals near buildings and trees; site and antenna choice help.
Clock: satellite and receiver clock errors; the clock term is estimated, and TDOP applies.
User dynamics: antenna motion, vibration and poor tracking at the survey pole.

blocks.text: DOP does not fix any of these. It only scales random range noise. A low PDOP with large multipath still gives a wrong fix. Planning uses a mask angle, the lowest elevation accepted; common values are 10° to 15°. A high mask removes noisy low satellites but may remove spread and raise DOP. Compute PDOP for the day and choose an observation window with low PDOP and enough satellites. In a city, plan around buildings. Multi-GNSS (GPS, GLONASS, Galileo, BeiDou and NavIC) adds satellites and usually lowers DOP. GPS modernization adds signals. See GPS and GNSS: principles and positioning methods for positioning.

examples.question: Two satellites are used in a 2D fix. From receiver R at (0,0), satellite A is at (0,10000) m and satellite B is at (10000,0) m. The unit vectors to A and B are (0,1) and (1,0). Form H and compute HDOP. What happens if B is at (0,20000) m instead?
steps: Receiver R = (0,0). Satellite A = (0,10000) m, so u<sub>A</sub> = (0,1). Satellite B = (10000,0) m, so u<sub>B</sub> = (1,0).
For the 2D unknown (x,y), use rows from the unit vectors. Rows are written here with +u instead of -u as in Section 1; the sign flip does not change HᵀH, so HDOP is the same. H = [[0,1],[1,0]].
The determinant is 0 × 2 − 0 × 0 = 0, so HᵀH is singular. HDOP is infinite: there is no horizontal spread between the two directions.
examples.answer: For the spread pair, HDOP = 1.414; for the collinear pair, HDOP is infinite.

examples.question: A receiver has a 1-sigma range error σ<sub>range</sub> = 3.0 m, and the planning software gives HDOP = 1.2 and VDOP = 2.0 for the observation window. Find the horizontal DRMS, the 2DRMS radius, the CEP for circular errors, and the 95 % vertical interval.
steps: Horizontal 1-sigma radial error: DRMS = HDOP × σ<sub>range</sub> = 1.2 × 3.0 = 3.6 m.
2DRMS = 2 × 3.6 = 7.2 m: about 95 % or more of the horizontal fixes lie within 7.2 m.
For circular errors σ<sub>x</sub> = σ<sub>y</sub> = σ, DRMS = σ√2 and CEP = 1.1774 σ, so CEP = 0.8326 × DRMS = 0.8326 × 3.6 = 3.0 m: half the fixes lie within 3.0 m.
Vertical 1-sigma error: σ<sub>v</sub> = VDOP × σ<sub>range</sub> = 2.0 × 3.0 = 6.0 m.
The vertical figure is larger than the horizontal one because all satellites are above the horizon, so height is the weakest coordinate.
examples.answer: DRMS 3.6 m, 2DRMS 7.2 m, CEP 3.0 m, and the 95 % vertical interval ±11.8 m.

traps: Treating high elevation as good geometry. DOP depends on how the line-of-sight directions are spread, not on elevation alone, not on signal strength and not on range distance.
Confusing DOP with accuracy. DOP scales random range noise; it does not remove ionosphere, multipath or ephemeris bias.
Saying CEP is 95%. CEP is about 50%; 2DRMS is the usual about-95% horizontal measure.
Forgetting the clock term. GDOP and TDOP include clock; HDOP and VDOP do not.
Assuming more satellites always lower DOP. A new satellite in the same cluster may barely change the geometry.

quiz.q: Define elevation angle and azimuth of a satellite.
quiz.a: Elevation is the angle above the horizon. Azimuth is the angle clockwise from north in the horizontal plane.

quiz.q: Why can four strong satellites with high elevation still give a large DOP?
quiz.a: High elevation alone does not spread the line-of-sight directions. If all satellites lie near one direction, HᵀH is nearly singular, so Q and DOP become large.

quiz.q: A receiver has σ_range = 0.5 m and HDOP = 1.8. Find the 1-sigma horizontal position error.
PDOP = 3 and σ_range = 2 m. Find the 1-sigma 3D position error.
A skyplot shows all satellites north and low. What happens to HDOP and VDOP, and what planning step helps?
quiz.a: North-only directions give weak east-west strength, so HDOP is large. Low elevation raises noise (more atmosphere and multipath). Here every satellite has almost the same low elevation, so the vertical and clock terms cannot be separated well and VDOP is also poor. The planning step is to wait for an observation window when satellites are spread in azimuth and in elevation, and to keep the mask angle low (10°–15°) so the low satellites that add spread are not rejected. A high mask angle here would remove the only satellites present.

quiz.q: State the difference between CEP and 2DRMS.
quiz.a: CEP is the radius containing about 50% of horizontal fixes. 2DRMS is about twice DRMS and is commonly used as an about-95% horizontal radius.

quiz.q: DOP is low, but check points are offset by 3 m from control. Give two likely causes.
quiz.a: Low DOP only means good geometry. A bias such as multipath at the site or an uncorrected atmospheric delay can shift all fixes. A wrong antenna height or a bad coordinate datum can also cause a constant offset.

quiz.q: Why can a very high mask angle worsen a GNSS survey?
quiz.a: It rejects low-elevation satellites. That can remove the only satellites giving horizontal spread, so PDOP or HDOP rises even though multipath and atmospheric noise fall.

beyond: Not for the exam. Multi-GNSS and precise point positioning now let a single receiver use many satellites and lower DOP without a base station. Modern receivers log PDOP with every point, so office software can flag weak fixes. Research looks at urban multipath and 3D-mapping-aided GNSS. Search next for GNSS skyplot, PDOP planning, NavIC, and 2DRMS confidence.
